# neatHack build log: Parallax

## Project

- **Name:** Parallax
- **Purpose:** an AI agency whose agents finish a research job end to end and check every answer from two independent angles before delivering it.
- **Problem:** research agents sound confident and are often wrong (stale headcount, a CEO who left last year, a "lead" who changed jobs). One source can't tell you it's wrong. Two independent sources that disagree can.

## Team

- neromtoobad (solo)

## Stack

- TypeScript, Node 24
- Models: neatHack LiteLLM gateway (claude-haiku, claude-sonnet-4.6, nova models)
- Tools: Crustdata APIs (company search/enrich, person search, web search, web fetch)
- neatlogs: traces for every job, agent step, tool call and model call
- Entire: checkpoints on every commit (branch `entire/checkpoints/v1`), entire-graph for code context
- cfo.ai: business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) from measured unit economics

## Build log

### 2026-10-11

- Read the rules. Planned the idea: a two-angle research agency (Records vs Field, an Arbiter, a Verifier and a CFO).
- Created the repo. Enabled Entire (Claude Code hooks, branch checkpoints) and entire-graph (`entire graph init-agents`).
- Wrote the agent core (server/): checkpointed steps, CFO quotes and budget caps, the two-angle company brief and lead list, and neatlogs spans. Typechecks; it has not run against live APIs yet because the keys aren't in.
- Followed Entire's neatHack guide (hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026): installed Entire Brain (`entire brain init-agents`, `entire brain setup`, which indexed 24 files and 257 symbols) and added the brain MCP server in `.mcp.json`.
- The first build session started outside the repo, before Entire's hooks existed, so it wasn't captured. That transcript also includes unrelated private notes, so it was not attached as a public checkpoint. The build continues in a fresh session opened in the repo, so every prompt and commit from here on is captured.

- First live job (company brief on Linear): it failed on a Crustdata 400 (a field name the API rejected), was fixed, then resumed from its checkpoint and delivered.
  - On the way it repaired a malformed model reply, and the Verifier rejected a web quote it could not find on the page, falling back to the database value.
  - Cost $0.161 against a $2 price.
  - neatlogs traces: `b0b16a50333cee82a2b6a842a258c667` (the failed run) and `313af6c8df2b296df7483c325d04f2ea` (the resumed run).
- Built the eval harness (`server/evals/cases.ts`, `scripts/eval.ts`, `scripts/compare.ts`): 7 company briefs with gold facts (founding year, CEO) and 2 lead lists. Every eval job is a normal traced job tagged `eval:<label>`.
- Ran the baseline eval `v1` and read its traces to find what to fix:
  - **The Verifier falsely rejected a correct CEO quote.** HTML-to-text drops spaces ("Karri SaarinenCo-founder"), so the quote check now ignores spacing.
  - **Field wasted credits on duplicate URLs** (`linear.app` and `linear.app/`) and on pages that block bots (Reddit). URLs are now canonicalised and those sites skipped.
  - **Field ran one fixed round of searches**, so facts missing after the first pass were never searched for. It now runs a second, targeted search per missing fact.
  - **The Writer padded the brief with guesses** ("likely", "will resonate"). The audit now rejects them.
- Web app (`web/`, Next.js): hire form with a CFO quote, a live job page (both angles side by side, verdicts, a streamed timeline, money against the budget cap, checkpoints, trace IDs), a jobs list, and a books page with eval comparisons.
  - Fixed live updates: Next's proxy gzip-buffered the event stream, so compression is now off for it.

- Lead-list fixes found by watching the v1 run:
  - **Bad candidates.** Semantic company search alone returned consultancies and courses. The search now uses hard headcount and country filters, and the database profiles are screened before any credits go on websites.
  - **Wrong contacts.** "CTO" substring-matched "Dire*cto*r", so a Senior Sales Director came back as a CTO lead. Titles now match on whole words, and the contact must hold the asked-for role or be a founder or C-level.
  - **Pages that wouldn't load.** Bot-check pages count as not loaded and get a browser-mode retry.
- Verifier fix: values naming several people. PostHog has two co-CEOs; the web said both and the database only one, and the old check wrongly rejected the web claim. Eval gold now accepts either co-CEO (posthog.com/about lists both).
- Two concurrency bugs, found when the API's crash recovery re-ran jobs the eval process was still working on:
  - **Leases.** A job carries the pid, host and time of its owner, and recovery only takes over a dead lease.
  - **Cache.** The job cache is keyed by file mtime, so a stale in-memory copy never looks abandoned.

### Eval v1 → v2 (same 9 fixed jobs; `server/evals/v1-vs-v2.md`)

| metric | v1 | v2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| facts seen from both angles | 45% | **82%** |
| facts verified | 100% | 100% |
| gold facts right / wrong | 14/14, 0 wrong | 14/14, 0 wrong |
| brief points with guesswork | 39% | **0%** |
| avg cost per brief | $0.167 | $0.189 (more searching, by design) |
| leads delivered / wanted | 9/10 (one list hit its budget) | **10/10** |
| candidates checked per lead | 6.9 | **2.0** |
| cost per delivered lead | $0.123 | **$0.072** |
| avg seconds per lead list | 231 | **113** |

Trace IDs for every row are in `server/evals/v1-vs-v2.md`.

### Recovery on production (unplanned)

- Live job `job_mv3ikdo86bu0` on Railway (company brief, Paystack) was running when two git pushes redeployed the container mid-job.
- The new container logged "The server restarted mid-job; resuming from the last saved step" and resumed as run 2 with **6 finished steps kept** (nothing paid twice).
- It rode out a string of Crustdata 429s with backoff, then delivered: 7/7 facts verified, cost $0.204, price $2.
- neatlogs traces: `1d2fd7e5055c87cd1015ba1082e2572f` (interrupted), `c45a78388a7d892fec0af7443a2fecb8` (resumed).

### Business plan

- `server/scripts/unit-economics.ts` → `docs/unit-economics.md`: measured cost per brief and per lead from delivered jobs. Data is about 90% of the cost; models 6–13%.
- `docs/business-plan-brief.md`: pricing, assumptions, scenarios and the prompt for cfo.ai (Ari). cfo.ai's MCP server is in `.mcp.json`.

Pending.

- [ ] Demo video, 3 min max, covering neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai

- [ ] Entire checkpoints / entire-graph output

Here's where Parallax stands as of Oct 11, 09:52. There are 25 commits, all made today, the working tree is clean and everything is pushed.

## What's built

**Agent core (`server/`)**
- Every job is one neatlogs workflow trace. Each step is checkpointed, so a job resumes from its last saved step and retries with backoff. A per-job budget cap pauses the job when it runs out, and it can be resumed after approval.
- Seven agents: Lead, CFO, Records (Crustdata database), Field (web search and fetch), Arbiter, Verifier and Writer.
- Seven services in three departments, all tested live:
  - **Sales:** `company-brief`, `lead-list`, `people-map`
  - **Market:** `competitor-teardown`, `market-map`
  - **Trust:** `vendor-check` (green/amber/red), `person-check`
- Hardening:
  - Job leases and an mtime-keyed cache, so crash recovery never runs the same job twice.
  - Pages are read for free first; Crustdata is paid only for pages that block us. Dead domains are skipped with a DNS check.
  - Chaos flags inject faults for recovery demos.

**Eval harness:** 7 company briefs and 2 lead lists with gold facts. Four versions have been run (v1 to v4), and every comparison is written up in `server/evals/`.

| | v1 | v4 |
|---|---|---|
| facts seen from both angles | 45% | 80% |
| gold facts right | 14/14 | 14/14 |
| brief points with guesswork | 39% | 0% |
| cost per brief | $0.167 | $0.155 |
| leads delivered | 9/10 | 10/10 |
| cost per delivered lead | $0.123 | $0.068 |
| seconds per lead list | 231 | 141 |

**Web app (`web/`, Next.js)**
- **Home:** live replay, departments, team and proof numbers.
- **Hire:** the form plus the CFO's quote.
- **Job page:** an illustrated "observatory" where 7 agent characters act out real job events. It shows the results, a money and activity sidebar, and an "Under the hood" section with saved steps and traces.
- **Jobs list** and **Books:** Books keeps client revenue separate from eval runs.

**Deploy:** it runs as one container on Railway. It has already recovered from a real crash in production: a redeploy hit the Paystack job mid-run, and it resumed with 6 steps kept and nothing paid twice.

**Business plan inputs:** `docs/unit-economics.md` holds cost per brief and per lead, measured from delivered jobs (data is about 90% of the cost). `docs/business-plan-brief.md` has pricing, scenarios and the prompt to give cfo.ai.

## What's left

1. **`hackathon.md` is behind.** Its log stops at the v2 eval and the business-plan inputs. It's missing the v3 and v4 evals, the UI overhaul and the five new services.
2. **The cfo.ai plan itself.** The brief is ready, but the plan hasn't been generated. The cfoai MCP server needs authorizing (via `/mcp` in a terminal session) before I can drive it.
3. **Entire evidence for the submission:** checkpoints and graph output, ready to show.
4. **Demo video** (3 minutes or less, covering neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai), plus the "Demo" and "Known limitations" sections of the log.
5. **Submission:** #neatHack posts, then quote-post the neatlogs post on Oct 12 between 13:30 and 18:25 UTC (14:30 to 19:25 your time).

# Parallax: business plan brief (input for cfo.ai)

This is the input we hand to cfo.ai (Ari) to build Parallax's financial model: pricing, costs, revenue and runway.
The unit costs are **measured**, not guessed: every model call and every Crustdata call in a job is metered as it happens, and the same calls appear as spans in that job's neatlogs trace.
Measured numbers live in [`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md); regenerate them with `node server/scripts/unit-economics.ts`.
Everything else below is an **assumption**, marked as such, for Ari to model and stress.

## The business

Parallax is an AI research agency for sales, partnerships and investing teams. Customers hire it per job:

- **Company brief.** Everything to know before a meeting, with every fact checked from two angles.
- **Lead list.** Companies that fit an ideal customer profile, each with the right person to contact, verified from two angles.

Customers are founders, SDRs/AEs, partnership leads and investors at small and mid-size companies.
The wedge is trust: other research agents hand you confident text, while Parallax shows where each fact came from and what it checked.

## Measured unit costs (from delivered eval jobs, Oct 11 2026)

| | Company brief | Lead list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost per unit, median | $0.168 per brief | $0.095 per delivered lead |
| Cost per unit, p75 (used for pricing) | $0.195 | $0.158 |
| Share of cost: data (Crustdata) / models | 87% / 13% | 94% / 6% |
| Crustdata credits per unit | 15.4 | 9.6 |
| Time per job, median | ~2 min | ~3.5 min for 5 leads |

These come from the v1 and v2 eval runs; they will be updated with v3 and live jobs.

**Cost drivers:**
- Data is about 90% of the variable cost. The model bill is small because extraction runs on Claude Haiku and only judgement and writing use Sonnet.
- The biggest lever is the Crustdata credit price (assumed below) and how many web searches and page reads each job makes.

## Pricing (proposal)

| Plan | Price | Includes | Gross margin at p75 cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay as you go: company brief | **$5 per brief** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: lead list | **$1 per verified lead** (you pay only for leads that pass) | – | 84% |
| Team (monthly) | **$99/mo** | 30 briefs + 150 verified leads | 70% if fully used; ~80% at typical 60% use |
| Pro (monthly) | **$299/mo** | 100 briefs + 500 verified leads | 67% if fully used |

The CFO agent prices each job from the 75th percentile of measured cost, at a 75% target margin. The public prices above sit well over that floor.

## Assumptions (for Ari to model; change freely)

| Assumption | Base | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crustdata cost per credit | $0.01 | Not published (sales-led pricing). Sensitivity: $0.005 / $0.02. |
| Model prices | list prices | Claude Haiku $1/$5 and Sonnet $3/$15 per M tokens (the hackathon gateway is free; production would pay these). |
| Hosting (Railway) | $20/mo | One container and a volume; grows with load. |
| Tracing (neatlogs) | $0 at first | Free tier is 100k spans/mo, and a job is about 30–80 spans, so roughly 1,500+ jobs/mo before upgrading. |
| Domain and email | $5/mo | |
| Payments | 5% of revenue | Merchant-of-record fee (e.g. Dodo Payments). |
| Founder | solo, no salary for the first 6 months | Then $3,000/mo. |
| Starting cash | $2,000 | Placeholder; set to real number. |

### Customer assumptions

| Scenario | Month 1 paying customers | Monthly growth | Mix | Monthly churn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 5 | 25% | 60% pay-as-you-go ($25/mo avg), 35% Team, 5% Pro | 6% |
| Growth | 10 | 40% | same | 4% |
| Downside | 3 | 10% | 80% pay-as-you-go | 10% |

## What we want from the model

1. A 24-month operating model per scenario: revenue by plan, variable cost (data + models + payment fees), gross margin, fixed costs, operating income, ending cash.
2. Runway in months for each scenario, and the month the business turns cash-flow positive.
3. Sensitivity of gross margin to the Crustdata credit price ($0.005 / $0.01 / $0.02) and to plan utilisation (40% / 60% / 100%).
4. When we can afford the first hire (a $5,000/mo engineer) without dropping below 6 months of runway.

## Prompt to paste into Ari

> Build a 24-month financial model for Parallax, an AI research agency that sells verified company briefs and lead lists to sales, partnership and investing teams. Use this unit economics:
> - a company brief costs us $0.195 to deliver (75th percentile, measured over real jobs; 87% data, 13% models);
> - a verified lead costs us $0.158 (94% data).
>
> Pricing:
> - $5 per brief pay-as-you-go;
> - $1 per verified lead;
> - Team plan $99/mo including 30 briefs + 150 leads;
> - Pro plan $299/mo including 100 briefs + 500 leads.
>
> Assume 60% plan utilisation, 5% payment fees, and fixed costs of $25/mo (hosting, domain), rising to $3,025/mo from month 7 when the founder starts drawing $3,000/mo. Starting cash $2,000. Model three scenarios:
> - **Base:** 5 customers in month 1, 25% monthly growth, 6% churn, mix 60% pay-as-you-go averaging $25/mo, 35% Team, 5% Pro.
> - **Growth:** 10 customers, 40% growth, 4% churn.
> - **Downside:** 3 customers, 10% growth, 10% churn, 80% pay-as-you-go.
>
> Show monthly revenue, gross margin, operating income, ending cash and runway per scenario, and the month each turns cash-flow positive. Add a sensitivity table of gross margin against data cost per credit ($0.005, $0.01, $0.02; base case is $0.01 and 15.4 credits per brief, 9.6 per lead) and plan utilisation (40%, 60%, 100%). Finally, tell me the earliest month we can hire a $5,000/mo engineer and keep at least 6 months of runway.

/**
 * Unit economics from real, delivered jobs: the numbers the cfo.ai business plan is built on.
 *
 *   node scripts/unit-economics.ts [--tags eval:v2,eval:v3,live-test]   → prints markdown, writes docs/unit-economics.json
 *
 * Every number comes from per-call metering (model tokens × list price, Crustdata credits from the
 * X-Credits-Used header), the same calls that appear as spans in each job's neatlogs trace.
 */
import { mkdirSync, readdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const tagArg = args[args.indexOf('--tags') + 1];
const tags = args.includes('--tags') ? tagArg.split(',') : null;

const root = join(import.meta.dirname, '../..');
const dir = join(root, 'data/jobs');
const jobs = readdirSync(dir)
  .filter((f) => f.endsWith('.json'))
  .map((f) => JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(dir, f), 'utf8')))
  .filter((j) => j.status === 'delivered' && (!tags || tags.includes(j.tag)));

const q = (xs: number[], p: number) => {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  return s.length ? s[Math.min(s.length - 1, Math.floor(s.length * p))] : 0;
};
const mean = (xs: number[]) => (xs.length ? xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / xs.length : 0);

const out: any = { generatedAt: new Date().toISOString(), tags, services: {} };
for (const service of ['company-brief', 'lead-list']) {
  const js = jobs.filter((j) => j.service === service);
  if (!js.length) continue;
  const units = (j: any) => (service === 'lead-list' ? Math.max(1, j.result?.stats?.verified ?? 0) : 1);
  const perUnit = js.map((j) => j.spend.totalUsd / units(j));
  const llmShare = mean(js.map((j) => j.spend.llmUsd / Math.max(1e-9, j.spend.totalUsd)));
  const secs = js.map((j) => (j.updatedAt - j.createdAt) / 1000);
  out.services[service] = {
    jobs: js.length,
    unit: service === 'lead-list' ? 'delivered lead' : 'brief',
    costPerUnit: { mean: mean(perUnit), p50: q(perUnit, 0.5), p75: q(perUnit, 0.75), max: Math.max(...perUnit) },

| Service | Unit | Jobs measured | Cost per unit, median | p75 (used for pricing) | Data / models | Crustdata credits per unit |

| Company brief | brief | 9 | $0.150 | **$0.161** | 79% / 21% | 12.3 |
| Lead list | verified lead | 6* | $0.096 | **$0.116*** | 93% / 7% | 11.1 |

| Competitor teardown | job | 4 | $0.184 | **$0.249** | 72% / 28% | 13.5 |

**Cost drivers:**
- Data is 72–96% of the variable cost. The model bill is small because extraction runs on Claude Haiku, and only judgement and writing use Sonnet.
- The biggest lever is the Crustdata credit price (assumed below). Parallax reads pages with its own fetch first (free) and pays Crustdata only for pages that block it. That change took a brief from $0.201 (v3) to $0.155 (v4) with the same accuracy.

| Pay as you go: person check | **$1** | – | 95% |

| Pro (monthly) | **$299/mo** | 100 briefs + 500 verified leads | 75% if fully used; 85% at 60% use |

- In the Team and Pro plans, the other services draw on the brief allowance. A people map, competitor teardown, market map or vendor check uses 1 brief, and a person check uses half of one. A teardown costs more than a brief ($0.249 against $0.161), so heavy teardown use lowers plan margins a little.
- Gross margins above are before payment fees.
- The CFO agent prices each one-off job from the 75th percentile of measured cost at a 75% target margin. The public prices above sit well above that floor.

# Parallax: business plan (cfo.ai)

Built by Ari (cfo.ai) on Oct 11 2026 from [`business-plan-brief.md`](business-plan-brief.md), which uses unit costs measured from real jobs ([`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md)).
The model lives in our cfo.ai workspace as four pages: Assumptions, Customers and Revenue, Cash and Hiring, and Cost Sensitivity, with Base, Growth and Downside scenarios.
It runs 24 months, from October 2026 to September 2028.

**Independent check.** We recomputed the three scenarios in a short script using the same conventions. Ari's headline numbers match ours to the dollar:
- month-24 revenue $17,652 / $761,425 / $134 (Base / Growth / Downside);
- Base's $7,716 funding gap;
- Base cash-flow positive again in month 15.

## Results before hiring

| | Base | Growth | Downside |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Month 24 monthly revenue | $17,652 | $761,425 | $134 |
| Gross margin (after delivery costs and 5% payment fees) | 82.6% | 82.6% | 84.0% |
| Month 24 operating income | $11,557 | $626,002 | −$2,912 |
| Month 24 ending cash | $37,327 | $2,322,242 | −$49,890 |
| First cash shortfall | month 9 | none | month 7 |
| Extra funding needed to stay above $0 | $7,716 | $0 | $49,890 |
| Cash-flow positive (from month 7, after the founder draw starts) | month 15 (Dec 2027) | throughout | never |

All three scenarios are cash-flow positive in months 1–6, before the founder draws a salary.

## What it says

- **The unit economics are strong.** Gross margin is about 83% after payment fees.
- **The founder's salary is what causes the cash gap.** In the Base case, a $3,000/mo draw from month 7 runs the $2,000 starting cash out in month 9. It needs a bridge of about $7.7k before profits return in month 15. The fix is to delay the draw, raise a small bridge, or grow faster.
- **First engineer ($5,000/mo):**
  - Only Growth can afford one. The earliest month is month 10 (July 2027), when the hire still leaves 6+ months of runway.
  - Ari's safer recommendation is month 13 (October 2027), when Growth also holds six months of fixed costs ($48,150) in cash.
  - Base and Downside can't fund the hire as modelled.
- **The data price is the biggest risk.** At 60% plan use, gross margin falls from 82.6% to 71.3% if Crustdata credits cost $0.02 instead of $0.01.

## Gross-margin sensitivity (Base mix, after payment fees)

| Data cost per credit | 40% plan use | 60% plan use | 100% plan use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0.005 | 90.2% | 88.3% | 84.4% |
| $0.010 | 86.2% | **82.6%** | 75.5% |
| $0.020 | 78.1% | 71.3% | 57.7% |

## Assumptions and limits

- Customers change each month by acquisition minus churn: 19% net growth in Base, 36% in Growth and 0% in Downside.
- **Growth is a stretch case**, not validated demand: it reaches about 11.8k customers by month 24.
- Pay-as-you-go revenue is split 50/50 between briefs and leads. In the plans, the other services use the brief allowance.
- Not included:
  - acquisition spend;
  - manual verification labour;
  - taxes, benefits and capacity limits.

  So this is not a fully loaded profitability claim.
- The newer services' costs come from only 1–4 measured jobs each (see the brief).

**Next questions for Ari:** how long can the founder draw be delayed in Base? How do acquisition and verification costs change the cash and hiring answers?

# Entire evidence

How Parallax used Entire during neatHack. Every file in this folder is the raw output of the command named in it, captured on Oct 11 2026 at commit `982d5ab`.

## Checkpoints

- Entire is enabled for Claude Code. Its hooks attach an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer to each commit, and a plain `git push` uploads the session transcripts to the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on GitHub.
- PII redaction is on for emails and phone numbers (`.entire/settings.json`).
- Captured so far:
  - **5 checkpoints on `main`** ([`checkpoints.txt`](checkpoints.txt)). Each links a prompt and its session transcript to the commit it produced.
  - **13 commits on `entire/checkpoints/v1`** ([`checkpoints-branch-log.txt`](checkpoints-branch-log.txt)).
  - **4 sessions**: this session, plus 3 sub-agent sessions attached at checkpoint `758532752575`. Those three did the background research and built the five newer services, about 28.6M tokens between them.

**Gap.** The commits from 07:15 to 09:52 on Oct 11 have no checkpoints. That covers the agent core, the evals, the web app and the UI overhaul. The sessions that wrote them were started from the parent folder (`~/Documents/Hacks`), not from inside the repo, so Entire's hooks never fired. Their git history and commit dates are intact; only the transcripts weren't captured. Every session since then runs inside the repo and is captured. This rule is now a durable fact in the Brain (see below).

## Graph: code structure

entire-graph builds a local code graph with no network access: 76 files, 923 symbols and 2,476 relations.

- **[`graph-search-resume.txt`](graph-search-resume.txt).** We asked in plain English: "resume a job from its last saved step after the server restarts". It returned the exact mechanism, ranked:
  1. `step()`, the checkpointed, retried and traced unit of work;
  2. `saveJob()`, which writes atomically and holds the lease;
  3. `createJob()`;
  4. `runJob()`, which logs "Resumed (run N); K finished steps kept".
- **[`graph-impact-step.txt`](graph-impact-step.txt).** The blast radius of changing `step()`: all 7 service runners call it, and it depends on `neatlogs.span`, `saveJob` and `emit`. This is the check we run before touching the checkpoint code.
- **[`graph-commit-36bd7cb.txt`](graph-commit-36bd7cb.txt).** An entity-level diff of the "five new services" commit. It lists which functions changed and how many dependents each has, which a line diff doesn't show.
- **[`graph-checkpoint-39e19d483791.txt`](graph-checkpoint-39e19d483791.txt).** The semantic changes behind one Entire checkpoint: the cfo.ai business plan.
- **[`graph-stats.txt`](graph-stats.txt).** An honest usage report. Across the captured sessions the agent made 8 graph calls and 132 plain grep/find/read calls. Most code discovery still went through grep; the graph was used for blast-radius and change analysis.

## Brain: repo memory

- **[`brain-overview.txt`](brain-overview.txt).** The Brain's summary of the repo: commands, key documents and entry points. It's built from the code, docs, git history and captured sessions, and a background daemon keeps it fresh every 5 minutes.
- **Durable facts** recorded with `entire brain remember` ([`brain-recall.txt`](brain-recall.txt) shows them being recalled):
  - **Session capture rule** (`workflow.capture.rule`): agent sessions must start inside the repo, or their commits get no checkpoints.
  - **Page reads** (`architecture.data.cost`): our own fetch first; Crustdata is paid only for blocked or thin pages.
  - **CFO pricing** (`architecture.pricing.rule`): quotes use the 75th-percentile cost of the last 12 jobs at a 75% target margin, with a floor until a service has 3 jobs.
- `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `.entire/agent-guide.md` tell every coding agent to start a task with `entire brain brief` and to use Graph for impact and diff checks.

content.text:
I ran a real company brief (Supabase) through the live Railway app and the whole flow works: quote, live run, results and the CFO's books. It also caught a factual bug, which I've fixed and committed locally as `ed8483f`. It isn't pushed, because pushing redeploys production.

**The flow:**
- **Home:** renders with no console errors; the replay and proof numbers show.
- **Hire:** the CFO quoted $2.00 with a $0.51 hard cap, and accepting started the job.
- **Job page:** the observatory animated during the run. It delivered in about 1.6 minutes for $0.165 against the $2 price, with 7 of 7 facts verified and 3 conflicts settled.
- **Write-up:** the Writer rejected one of its own drafts for using a number not in the facts.
- **Jobs and Books:** both work. Books takes about 5 seconds to load.

**The bug:** the result said Supabase is headquartered in Singapore. The database said US and the web said San Francisco, but the Arbiter, which settles conflicts between the two, chose Singapore because Supabase's terms of service name a Singapore legal entity. The Arbiter now gets a definition with each fact it settles, and for headquarters that rules out place of incorporation. The same brief run locally now says San Francisco, and the typecheck passes. The eval only checks founding year and CEO, which this change doesn't touch, so I didn't re-run it.

**Decisions before the demo:**
1. **Push the fix?** The live site has the bug until you do. Pushing redeploys Railway, which takes about 2 minutes, and nothing is running there now.
2. **Price mismatch.** The live CFO quotes $2 per brief, but the business plan says $5. On camera that looks inconsistent. Either raise the app's minimum brief price to $5, a one-line change, or call $2 the launch price in the plan.
3. **Production has almost no history.** It holds two jobs, so Books looks thin and the quotes for the other six services use starting estimates. The 24 measured jobs live only on this machine. Options: run a handful of jobs on production (about $1–2 in credits), or record the Books and evals parts of the demo from a local copy.

There's also a smaller issue: the Writer built on the bad HQ ("a presence in the Asia-Pacific market"). The audit only looks for hedging words, so it doesn't catch inferences like that. It's in the build log as still open.

# Demo script (3:00 max)

The rule: cover **neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai**, all three on screen. One idea per scene. The voiceover lines are short so they fit the timing; read them, don't ad-lib.

App: https://parallax-production-b5e6.up.railway.app

## Before recording

- [ ] **Browser:** 1280×800 window, light theme, zoom 100%, bookmarks bar hidden. Sign in to neatlogs, cfo.ai and GitHub first.
- [ ] **Tabs open, in order:**
  1. app home
  2. app hire page for company brief
  3. a delivered job page
  4. neatlogs trace of that job
  5. app Books
  6. GitHub repo, `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch
  7. terminal with `entire checkpoint list` and `entire graph impact` ready
  8. cfo.ai share link
- [ ] **Job to show live:** pick a company not used before (e.g. Resend, Clerk, PostHog). A brief takes about 80–100 s, so record the run in full, then speed it up 3–4× in the edit.
- [ ] **Recovery clip, recorded locally:**
  1. Start `npm run dev` in `server/` and the web app.
  2. Start a brief.
  3. After 3–4 steps, Ctrl+C the server, then restart it.
  4. The job page shows "Resumed (run 2); N finished steps kept".

  Optionally set `PARALLAX_CHAOS="crust:0.3"` so retries show in the activity feed.

## Scenes

| # | Time | On screen | Voiceover |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0:00–0:15 | Home hero: "Research you can actually trust" | "AI research agents sound sure of themselves and are often wrong. One source can't tell you it's wrong. Two independent sources that disagree can. That's Parallax." |
| 2 | 0:15–0:30 | Hire page: type a company and purpose, click Get a quote; CFO card shows $5 and a hard cap | "You hire it like an agency. The CFO agent quotes from what similar jobs really cost, and sets a hard budget nobody can spend past." |
| 3 | 0:30–1:00 | Job page, observatory animating (sped up); activity feed shows Records and Field working | "Seven agents. Records reads the databases. Field reads the open web. Neither sees the other's answer. When they disagree, the Arbiter goes looking for a tiebreak." |
| 4 | 1:00–1:20 | Results: "Two angles, side by side" table with *both agree* / *settled* verdicts; scroll to the write-up | "Every fact ships with where it came from. The Verifier checks each quote is really on the page, and the Writer's draft gets sent back if it guesses." |
| 5 | 1:20–1:45 | **neatlogs**: the job's trace, WORKFLOW → AGENT steps → TOOL calls (Crustdata) → LLM calls, with cost | "Every job is one neatlogs trace: each agent step, each data call, each model call. That's how we found what to fix…" |
| 6 | 1:45–2:00 | Books / `server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md` table | "…same nine test jobs, four versions. Guesswork in briefs: 39% to zero. Cost per verified lead: 12 cents to 7. Fourteen of fourteen known facts right, every version." |
| 7 | 2:00–2:20 | Recovery clip: kill server mid-job → restart → "Resumed (run 2); 6 finished steps kept" | "Every step is a checkpoint. Kill the server mid-job and it picks up where it stopped. Nothing gets paid for twice. This happened for real on production when a deploy hit a running job." |
| 8 | 2:20–2:40 | **Entire**: `entire checkpoint list`, the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on GitHub, then `entire graph impact step` showing all 7 services depend on it | "The build itself is checkpointed with Entire. Prompts and transcripts are linked to commits. Its code graph shows what breaks if we touch the checkpoint code." |
| 9 | 2:40–3:00 | **cfo.ai**: Cash and Hiring page, then the sensitivity table | "And the business: cfo.ai built the plan from our measured unit costs. 83% gross margin. The risk is data prices; the founder's salary is what needs a bridge. Parallax: research you can actually trust." |

## Numbers to say (all from the repo)

- **Eval v1 → v4** (`server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md`):
  - gold facts 14/14 right in every version;
  - guesswork 39% → 0%;
  - cost per verified lead $0.123 → $0.068;
  - facts seen from both angles 45% → 80%.
- **Production recovery:** job `job_mv3ikdo86bu0` resumed with 6 steps kept. neatlogs traces `1d2fd7e5…` (interrupted) and `c45a7838…` (resumed).
- **cfo.ai** (`docs/business-plan.md`):
  - gross margin 82.6%;
  - the Base case needs a ~$7.7k bridge and turns cash-flow positive in month 15;
  - with credits at $0.02, margin falls to 71.3%.

## Don't

- Show `.env`, API keys or the Railway variables page.
- Show the cfo.ai workspace sidebar, which shows another workspace name; use the share link instead.
- Claim the whole build is in Entire. The 07:15–09:52 commits have no checkpoints (`docs/entire/README.md`).

**Three issues to sort out before recording:**
1. **Three live prices don't match the business plan:**
   - The lead list quotes $2 for 5 leads, where the plan says $1 per verified lead, so $5.
   - The teardown quotes $4 against the plan's $5.
   - The market map quotes $2 for 8 companies against about $2.40.

   Fixing all three means giving lead lists and market maps a per-unit minimum price, plus a one-line change for teardowns. It's small. Should I do it?
2. **Books counts one of my test runs as client revenue.** When I checked the live app, I hired the Supabase brief through the normal form, and it went in untagged. Books shows it as "1 client job, $2.00 revenue", which isn't true, and there's no way to re-tag it through the app. Options: add a small admin route to re-tag it, or just don't show the "client revenue" figure in the demo.
3. **Small oddities to look at:**
   - The teardown names the company "Clay Automation". The competitors it found are right for Clay, so it's probably just the database's name for it, but I'd check the result page before showing it on camera.
   - The Resend brief says founded 2023. Resend went through YC's Winter 2023 batch, so 2022 is also plausible; avoid that one on camera.

You can search, purchase, and manage domains without leaving Railway. DNS is auto-configured, WHOIS privacy is included, and auto-renewal is on by default.

By default, Railway fully manages DNS for purchased domains through its own nameservers, so pointing a domain at a Railway service needs no manual configuration. Open a domain from [railway.com/workspace/domains](https://railway.com/workspace/domains) to view its nameservers and DNS records.

### Nameservers

When a domain uses Railway's nameservers, the **Nameservers** section shows "Railway is managing DNS for this domain" and Railway maintains the zone for you.

To host DNS with an external provider instead — for example, to use Cloudflare's proxy/WAF, Amazon Route 53, or another third-party DNS host — a workspace admin can delegate the domain to that provider **without transferring it out of Railway**:

1. Open the domain from [railway.com/workspace/domains](https://railway.com/workspace/domains).
2. In the **Nameservers** section, click **Use Custom Nameservers**.
3. Enter the nameserver hostnames your DNS provider gave you (most providers give you two; up to four are supported), then save.

To return to Railway-managed DNS at any time, click **Reset to Railway**.

<Banner variant="warning">
While a domain is delegated to an external provider, Railway no longer controls its zone, which changes how you attach it to a service and manage its records.
</Banner>

Specifically, while custom nameservers are in use:

- The one-click **Add a custom domain** flow no longer lists this domain in service settings. You can still attach it using the [standard custom domain flow](/networking/domains/working-with-domains#custom-domains) — add the domain on your service, then create the `CNAME`/`ALIAS` records Railway provides at your external DNS host.
- The **DNS records** section no longer lists records. It shows "DNS records are managed at your external provider" and the add-record button is disabled, so manage records at your provider instead.

Only workspace admins can change a domain's nameservers, and only while the domain is active.

### DNS records

While Railway manages your nameservers, the **DNS records** section lists every DNS record for the domain, and admins can add, edit, and remove records directly. If you delegate the domain to an external provider with [custom nameservers](#nameservers), the section stops listing records and instead shows "DNS records are managed at your external provider" with the add-record button disabled.

## Transfer a domain to another registrar

Workspace admins can transfer a Railway-purchased domain to another registrar directly from the domain's detail page. Transferring out **requires two-factor authentication (2FA)** and is available only on active domains.

<Banner variant="info">
If you only need Cloudflare's proxy/WAF or DNS hosted elsewhere, you don't need to transfer your domain out — use [custom nameservers](#nameservers) instead.
</Banner>

### 60-day transfer lock

ICANN places a 60-day lock on every newly registered or newly transferred domain, so a Railway-purchased domain can't be transferred out until 60 days after it was registered. This is an ICANN policy that Railway cannot waive or expedite.

Until the domain is eligible, the **Transfer to Another Registrar** section shows the date it becomes eligible, in your local timezone.

### Start a transfer

Once the domain is eligible, a workspace admin can start the transfer:

1. Open the domain from [railway.com/workspace/domains](https://railway.com/workspace/domains) and find the **Transfer to Another Registrar** section.
2. Click **Get Transfer Code**. A confirmation dialog explains that starting the transfer unlocks the domain at the registrar, turns off auto-renewal, and provides a transfer authorization (EPP) code.
3. Confirm and complete 2FA.
4. Copy the **EPP/auth code** and paste it at your new registrar to start the transfer there.

After you start a transfer:

- **Most transfers complete in 5-7 days.** The transfer is carried out by the gaining registrar, not Railway.
- **Auto-renewal is turned off**, so you won't be billed again at the end of the current term.
- **If you lose the code**, return to this section and click **Get Transfer Code** again — it returns the same code.
- **Make sure before you start — transfers are final.** Once started, a transfer won't be undone; the domain moves to your new registrar, where you'll manage it from then on.

## Email forwarding

Forward mail sent to an address on your Railway-purchased domain to an inbox you already use. Railway doesn't create a mailbox or store your mail. Each message is relayed to the destination you choose.

Open a domain from [railway.com/workspace/domains](https://railway.com/workspace/domains) and find the **Email Forwarding** section, next to **DNS records**. Only workspace admins can add, edit, and remove addresses.

1. Click **Add Address**.
2. Enter the address to forward, such as `hello`, and the destination inbox it should reach.
3. Open the actions menu for the address, then click **Send test email** to confirm it arrives.

Enabling forwarding adds seven DNS records to the domain apex, several mail exchange records and one sender policy record, which appear alongside your other [DNS records](#dns-records). Forwarding depends on the mail exchange records. While forwarding addresses exist, Railway refuses both a mail exchange record for another provider at the domain apex and delegation to [custom nameservers](#nameservers).

### Before you rely on forwarding

Forwarding hands each message to an inbox you already own, which shapes what it can do:

- Replies come from the destination inbox and show that address, not the address the mail was sent to.
- Spam isn't filtered on the way through. The destination inbox applies its own filtering, so check its spam folder.
- Messages with attachments over 10 MB may fail to arrive.
- Each address forwards to one destination. Catch-all and wildcard addresses aren't supported.
- Mail sent from the destination inbox to the forwarded address isn't forwarded back, so test with **Send test email** rather than emailing yourself.

### Address limits

Each domain can have a limited number of forwarding addresses, set by your workspace plan:

| Trial | Free | Hobby | Pro | Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 5 | 25 | 25 |

The limit counts per domain and applies when you add an address.

### When forwarding isn't available

Railway offers forwarding only on domains whose mail records it can manage. The **Email Forwarding** section shows guidance instead of a form when:

- The domain already sends or receives mail through another provider. Set forwarding up with that provider, because adding it in Railway would break your existing setup.
- DNS is delegated to [custom nameservers](#nameservers). Set forwarding up at that provider, or reset to Railway's nameservers first.

## Billing

Domain subscriptions are separate from your workspace subscription.

- Priced at cost, rounded to dollar
- First-year price may differ from the renewal price
- You receive a notification before an upcoming renewal
- Auto-renewal charges approximately 30 days before expiration
- If payment fails, Railway retries up to three times before the domain expires

## FAQ

Common questions about Railway Domains.

<Collapse title="Can I transfer a domain between workspaces?">
Not yet. This capability is planned.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I transfer a domain out of Railway?">
Yes. Workspace admins can transfer a Railway-purchased domain to another registrar from the domain's detail page (2FA required). A domain can't be transferred until 60 days after registration, per ICANN policy. See [Transfer a domain to another registrar](#transfer-a-domain-to-another-registrar).
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I transfer a domain into Railway?">
No. Railway doesn't support transferring in a domain registered with another registrar. To use a domain you own elsewhere, add it to your service as a [custom domain](/networking/domains/working-with-domains#custom-domains) — it stays registered where it is.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I use Cloudflare or another DNS provider with my domain?">
Yes. Workspace admins can point a Railway-purchased domain at an external DNS provider with [custom nameservers](#nameservers), without transferring the domain out. While custom nameservers are in use, the one-click custom domain flow is disabled and DNS records are managed at your external provider instead of in Railway.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I get email on my domain?">
Railway can forward mail sent to an address on your domain to an inbox you already use. It doesn't host mailboxes, so you can't read mail in Railway or send from the forwarded address. See [Email forwarding](#email-forwarding).
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Which TLDs are available?">
Over 250 popular TLDs. No restricted or country-code TLDs requiring local presence.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I buy a domain without attaching it to a service?">
Yes. Purchase a domain and connect it to a service later.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="What happens if renewal payment fails?">
Railway retries payment up to three times before the domain expires.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Can I manually configure DNS records?">
Yes, while Railway manages your nameservers you can add or remove any DNS record for the domain. If you switch to [custom nameservers](#nameservers), manage records at your external provider instead.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Who is the registrant contact for my domain?">
Railway is listed as the registrant contact. We handle all registry and ICANN communications on your behalf.
</Collapse>

**An AI agency that checks every answer from two angles.**

Research agents sound sure of themselves and are often wrong: stale headcounts, a CEO who left last year, a "lead" who changed jobs. One source can't tell you it's wrong. Two independent sources that disagree can.

Parallax is a team of agents you hire for a research job. They do the whole job, start to finish, and every fact is seen from two angles and checked at its source before it reaches you.

# neatlogs evidence

Every Parallax job is one neatlogs trace:
- a `WORKFLOW` root per job run, named after its service;
- an `AGENT` span for each checkpointed step;
- a `TOOL` span for every Crustdata or web call;
- an `LLM` span for every model call, with token counts.

There are 80 traces in the project so far. Screenshots were taken from the neatlogs dashboard on Oct 11 2026.

## One job, end to end

[`trace-company-brief.jpg`](trace-company-brief.jpg) shows a company brief on Supabase, run on production (trace `243dde8738e16400ad66976315600f01`).
- 36 steps in 98 s.
- Lead plans the job, Records calls the Crustdata databases, Field runs web searches and page reads, then the Arbiter, Verifier and Writer take over.
- This run caught a real bug: the Arbiter picked a legal entity as the headquarters. The trace showed which tiebreak source it used, and the fix is in the build log.

## Crash recovery on production

A live job (company brief on Paystack, `job_mv3ikdo86bu0`) was running when two git pushes redeployed the container.

| | Trace | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`recovery-1-interrupted.jpg`](recovery-1-interrupted.jpg) | `1d2fd7e5055c87cd1015ba1082e2572f` | Run 1: Lead intake → Records → Field (web searches, page fetches, extractions) → Arbiter, then the container was replaced |
| [`recovery-2-resumed.jpg`](recovery-2-resumed.jpg) | `c45a78388a7d892fec0af7443a2fecb8` | Run 2 (`Run: 2` in the input) starts at the Arbiter's tiebreaks. Intake, Records and Field are **not** re-run, because their checkpointed results were kept. It ends with the Verifier and Writer and delivers 7/7 facts verified for $0.204 |

## Before and after

The eval runs are traced and tagged `eval:v1` … `eval:v4`, and every eval job's trace ID is listed in `server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md`. Reading the v1 traces is how we found:
- the Verifier rejecting a correct quote (spacing lost in HTML-to-text);
- Field paying twice for duplicate URLs;
- one-pass searches that left facts missing;
- a Writer that padded briefs with guesses.

## Detections

neatlogs flagged two of this morning's production jobs as **Execution Failed**, though both delivered:
- **People map on Linear** (trace `cc419daffbf780171c90c856fbe1cc39`). One `crustdata.web_search` errored after 39.4 s while checking one person on the web. The job carried on: that person was kept on the database's word and reported as not web-confirmed ("4 of 5 confirmed on the open web").
- **Vendor check on stripe.com** (`job_mv3o65hg0naz`). Also flagged; it delivered green, with 12 of 13 checks passed.

Next fix: retry a web search once on timeout before counting a person as unconfirmed.

content.text:
I pushed it (`2b7354b`). Production redeploys in a couple of minutes, and nothing is running there right now.

The retry fix turned up two bugs, both now fixed:

1. **Crustdata rate limits, not timeouts.** The people map's activity log shows the web search failed on three 429 responses in a row. That's Crustdata's rate limit, which I hit because 4–7 test jobs were sharing the key. The code already retried, but gave up after about 36 seconds. On rate limits it now tries up to 6 times, about 90 seconds in total.
2. **A false "server restarted mid-job" message.** The same log showed this line with no restart behind it. The once-a-minute recovery check treated jobs still running in the same process as abandoned. Nothing ran twice, but every job longer than a minute got that line in its activity feed, which would have looked wrong on camera. Recovery now skips jobs the process is actively running.

**Checked:** the typecheck passes. I also ran a real 124-second company brief through a local server, through two of those recovery checks, and it delivered with no false recovery line (about $0.15 in credits). I didn't reproduce the rate-limit case, since that would mean flooding Crustdata on purpose. That change only affects how long it keeps retrying.

Both fixes are written up in [docs/neatlogs/README.md](docs/neatlogs/README.md), as findings from reading the trace.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/mac/.claude/skills/ui-motion-reel

# UI motion reel

A reel is one HTML scene rendered frame by frame. Every animated value (shape size, radius, colour, camera zoom, cursor, controls) is a damped spring simulated once up front at 8x the frame rate, so any frame can be rendered independently and in parallel. The score is synthesised from the same timeline, so every beat, click and whoosh lines up with the picture.

The bundled pieces:

- `assets/engine/reel.js`: the engine (springs, measurement, cursor script, camera, content blur-swaps, hover and press, seamless loop, odometer counters, the icon set).
- `assets/engine/score.js`: an original loopable track (pads, plucked arpeggio, bass, drums, risers, bells) plus UI sound design (clicks, whooshes, typing, detents, swipes), rendered with OfflineAudioContext.
- `assets/template/index.html`: a 24 s starter scene with every interaction type: list with row hovers, slider drag, toggle, odometer, hold-to-confirm ring, success pill, summary card, loop back.
- `scripts/setup.sh`: scaffolds a reel folder (engine + template + scripts + node deps).
- `scripts/render.mjs`: stills, audio, and a parallel MP4 render with the score muxed and loudness-normalised.
- `scripts/qa.mjs`: contact sheet, raw loop-seam check, transition strips, loudness and spectrogram.
- `references/api.md`: the full `Reel.define` config reference. Read it before writing a scene.
- `references/craft.md`: the motion and design rules, and the mistakes that were already made and fixed. Read it before designing states.
- `references/score.md`: how to shape the music and sound design, and how to check a mix you cannot hear.
- `references/examples/stockback.html`: the original 60 s, 14-state reel this skill was extracted from (a fintech receipt-to-stocks app). Read it for content ideas and denser choreography. It predates the engine API, so copy patterns, not code.

## Workflow

1. **Learn the product first.** Read the product's site or code for its palette, fonts, logo, and the 5-8 moments that tell its story (the input, the "magic", the proof, the payoff). Pull real copy and real data where you can: real numbers and real logos make the reel believable. If the user asked for a specific look, that wins over the product's own look.

2. **Script the states before you write markup.** For each state decide its size (w, h, radius), fill (one of 3-4 palette colours), camera zoom (so it fills about 80% of the frame height or width), duration, and what the cursor does. Aim for 45-60 s and 10-14 states for a full reel, or 20-30 s and 5-7 states for a teaser. At 120 BPM a beat is 0.5 s and a bar is 2 s. Make every state's duration a multiple of 0.5 s and put the big moments on bar lines (multiples of 2 s) so the music can hit them. Durations must add up exactly to the total.

3. **Scaffold.** `bash ~/.claude/skills/ui-motion-reel/scripts/setup.sh <project>/video`, then edit `<project>/video/index.html`. Keep the engine files unmodified unless the reel needs an engine feature; if so, change the copy in the project and mention it.

4. **Build the scene** following `references/api.md`: one `.content` block per state (`id="c-<id>"`, `data-w`/`data-h` equal to the state's w/h), ids on everything the cursor targets or you animate, then `Reel.define({...})` with states, cursor events, custom channels (sliders, toggles, holds, scrubs) and per-state `update` functions for inner animation.

5. **Review stills early and often.** `node render.mjs --stills 0,1.5,4,...` then look at them (build a contact sheet with `node qa.mjs --every 2`). Check every state at rest and a few mid-morph frames. Rendering stills takes seconds; a full render takes about a minute and a half for 60 s on 6 workers.

6. **Score it.** Set `score` (progression, hits on the key states, breaks) and an `sfx` hook for scene-specific sounds (typing, detents, counters, swipes). `node render.mjs --audio`, then `node qa.mjs` and read the loudness line and `out/qa/spectrum.png` (see `references/score.md`: you cannot listen, so you judge the mix by numbers and pictures).

7. **Render and QA.** `node render.mjs --mp4 --with-audio --out <name>.mp4`, then `node qa.mjs --transitions --video out/<name>.mp4`. Confirm the raw loop seam is 1.000000, look at `transitions.png` for grey mid-morphs or content spilling off-frame, and look at the contact sheet once more.

8. **Deliver** the MP4 (and a 720p copy if a file transfer might struggle with size), plus a short list of what's in it: states, interactions, what the music does. Tell the user honestly that you checked the audio by analysis, not by ear. Offer to retime or re-theme: a re-render is cheap.

## Non-negotiables (the look)

These are what make it read as a designer's reel rather than a template. `references/craft.md` explains each one.

- One shape, never cut. Every state is the same element changing size, radius and fill; content swaps inside it with a short blur (the engine does this).
- A cursor causes every change: a click, a drag, or a press-and-hold. No state changes by itself unless it's a genuine system response (a hold completing).
- Springs everywhere; at most a tiny overshoot (zeta around 0.86 for size, 1.0 for colour and camera). No bouncy easing.
- The camera fits each state; the last frame equals the first so the reel loops.
- No dead time: something meaningful moves at every moment, and the cursor never waits more than about a second.
- No particle bursts, glows, lens flares, gradients on UI chrome, or mismatched icon strokes (use the engine's icon set: one 24 grid, one 1.75 stroke).
- One UI typeface, optionally with one display accent (the template pairs Geist with Instrument Serif italics). Use the product's fonts when it has them.

## Performance notes

- A 60 s reel at 1080p60 is 3,600 frames. With 6 workers it renders in about 80-90 s on an Apple-silicon Mac.
- The scripts call `process.exit` at the end because puppeteer can keep Node alive after the work is done. If you write your own scripts, do the same, or long commands will look hung.
- On networks where large uploads time out, also export a 720p copy: `ffmpeg -i reel.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720 -c:v libx264 -crf 25 -c:a aac -b:a 160k reel-720p.mp4` (ffmpeg is at `node_modules/@ffmpeg-installer/*/ffmpeg`).

Design type at 14-40px and let the zoom do the rest. 24 - Every element the cursor targets, or that you animate from `update`, needs an `id` (ids must be unique across all states). Higher omega is faster; zeta 1 is critically damped (no overshoot), 0.86 overshoots about 1%. 49 50 ## States 51 52 ```js 53 { id: 'settings', w: 580, h: 520, r: 32, fill: 'paper', zoom: 1.55, dur: 5.0, 54 advance: 'click', // default: an automatic click lands at dur-0.13 s and the next state starts at dur 55 cursor: [ ...events ] } 56 ``` 57 58 - `advance: 'click'` (default) presses wherever the cursor is at the end of the state. Move the cursor onto the state's primary button about 1 s before the end, so it arrives, the button shows its hover state, then gets pressed. 59 - `advance: 'hold'` for a press-and-hold state: add a `hold` event that releases just before `dur`. 60 - `advance: 'none'` for a state that ends by itself (use sparingly). The last state is always `none`: give it `dur: null` so it fills to the end, and make it the same size, fill, zoom and content as state 0 so the loop closes. 61 - `fill`: a name from `fills`, or a function of the state API returning one, for a colour flip inside a state (a night-mode toggle, a success tint after a click): `fill: (a) => (a.clicked('#night') ? 'night' : 'paper')`. State 0's function is called with the API at t = 0. 62 - `zoom`: aim for the state to fill about 80% of 1080 in height, or about 75% of 1920 in width. Roughly `min(1500 / w, 870 / h)`. 63 64 ## Cursor events (times are seconds from the state's start) 65 66 ```js 67 ['move', 0.5, target] // start moving to target (spring; arrives in about 0.6 s) 68 ['click', 3.0] // press + release where the cursor is; the engine records what it hit 69 ['drag', 0.9, 2.3, fromTarget, toTarget] // press, travel from->to on a smootherstep path, release 70 ['hold', 0.35, 1.9] // press and hold (drives a hold ring through a channel) 71 ``` 72 73 After a drag the cursor stays at the drop point. You don't need an extra `move`. 74 75 Targets: `[x, y]` in world px; `'#id'` (centre of the element); `{ sel: '#id', dx, dy }` (offset from centre); `{ along: '#track', f: 0.6, dy }` (a fraction across an element, for slider tracks and charts). 76 77 ## Channels and the `a` API 78 79 A channel is your own spring. Its `target(a)` runs 480 times a second; return a number to set the target, or `null` to keep the previous one. 80 81 ```js 82 channels: { 83 slider: { init: 0.3, w: 40, target: (a) => (a.dragging('settings') ? a.dragFrac('#st-track') : null) }, 84 notify: { init: 0, w: 20, z: 0.9, target: (a) => (a.clicked('#st-tog') ? 1 : null) }, 85 hold: { init: 0, w: 9, target: (a) => (a.state === 'hold' ? a.holdProgress('hold') : null) }, 86 } 87 ``` 88 89 In the last state every channel springs back to `init`, so the loop closes. Set `reset: false` on a channel to opt out. 90 91 `hover` vs `press`: `hover` elements get an automatic background tint and depress on click. Put anything whose background is state-driven (toggles, selectable chips, segmented options) in `press` instead and colour it yourself in `update`; otherwise the hover tint overwrites your colour. Transparent elements are never tinted. 92 93 `a` provides: 94 - `t`, `lt` (time in state), `state` (id), `si` (index), `last`, `cursor` `{x, y}`, `pressed`, `M` (measurements). 95 - `dragging(stateId?)`: the active drag, or null. 96 - `dragFrac('#track')`: the cursor's 0..1 position across an element. 97 - `clicked('#id')`: whether a click has landed on that element yet. Clicks resolve to the pressable (`hover` or `press` list) under the cursor at click time. 98 - `clickedIn(stateId, n)`: at least n clicks in that state. 99 - `holding()`, `holdProgress(stateId)`: 0..1 across the hold. 100 - `hovering('#id')`. 101 102 Because controls read the real cursor position, the knob sits under the cursor for the whole drag. At `w: 40` a knob trails a fast drag by about 25 px, which reads as lag. Toggles and number rolls want softer springs (`w` 16-22, `z` around 0.9) so they settle with character. 103 104 ## update(lt, S, h) 105 106 Called for each visible state on every rendered frame. `lt` is the time since the state started, `S` holds the frame's channel values (`S.slider`, `S.hold`, plus `S.w`, `S.zoom`, `S.cx`...), and `h` provides helpers: `h.el(id)`, `h.sp`, `h.ease`, `h.clamp`, `h.lerp`, `h.mix`, `h.rgb`, `h.setOdo(el, value, decimals, lineHeight)`, `h.hover('#id')`, `h.fill('accent')`. 107 108 Patterns (all in the template or the Stockback example): 109 - **Staggered reveal:** `const k = h.sp(lt - 0.3 - i * 0.14, 15, 0.9); row.style.opacity = k; row.style.transform = translateY((1-k)*10px)`. 110 - **Line-by-line print** (receipts, code): `clipPath: inset(0 (1-ease(k))*100% 0 0)` per line, with a thin scan bar sweeping down. 111 - **Draw a stroke:** give the path `pathLength="1" stroke-dasharray="1 1"`, then animate `strokeDashoffset` from 1 to 0. 112 - **Odometer:** `Reel.odo(el, '$0.000')` once, then `h.setOdo(el, value, 3, lineHeightPx)` each frame. The lower digits roll and carry into the higher ones. 113 - **Typing:** slice a string by elapsed time, with a caret that stays solid while typing and blinks at rest. 114 - **Number swap** (currency, units): two absolutely positioned spans crossing vertically, with `blur(k*(1-k)*16px)` at the midpoint. 115 - **Buttons appearing:** `opacity = sp(...)` plus `style.translate = 0 (1-k)*14px`. Use the `translate` property rather than `transform`, because the engine owns `transform` for the press. 116 117 ## Globals for the renderer 118 119 `window.READY` (a promise), `window.renderFrame(f)`, `window.TOTAL_FRAMES`, `window.FPS`, `window.renderAudio()` (resolves to `{ wav: base64, peak }`), and `window.__starts` (state start times, used by QA transition strips). 1 # Craft: what makes the reel look expensive 2 3 These rules came from building and critiquing a real 60 s reel frame by frame. Each has a reason; keep the reason in mind when a new product tempts you to bend a rule. 4 5 ## Story before pixels 6 7 - Use 10-14 states for 60 s. Each state is one idea a viewer can read in 3-6 s: input → the smart step → the user's control → the commitment (hold) → proof (confirmation) → payoff (numbers) → trust (safety, under the hood) → business (how it earns) → brand lockup. 8 - The lockup's call-to-action button is the loop point. Clicking it collapses the whole shape into the very first state, so the loop reads as intentional. 9 - Use real content: the product's real copy, real numbers, real logos, a real transaction hash. Placeholder lorem reads as a template instantly. 10 - One accent word per headline in the display face (for example "Who *profits*", "Injection *ignored*"). Don't italicise whole sentences. 11 12 ## The shape 13 14 - It's one element, and it never cuts or cross-fades. It changes width, height, radius and fill, and content swaps inside it with a short blur: about 0.11 s out, then in from 0.1 s after the switch. 15 - Alternate light and dark states (paper → ink → paper → accent → success) so every transition has visible energy. Two paper states in a row need a big size change to feel like a move. 16 - **Colour springs must be fast** (omega 30, critically damped). At omega 12, a white→black morph sat mid-grey for 0.3 s and looked muddy. At 30 it passes through grey in about 2 frames. 17 - Radius tracks the shape (pill → card → circle); clamp it to half the smaller side. The engine does this. 18 - Keep shadows soft and tinted to the palette, with a 1px hairline. No glow. 19 20 ## The camera 21 22 - Zoom so each state fills about 80% of the frame. The camera doesn't pan; it leans slightly toward the cursor (4.5% of the cursor's offset), which is enough to feel hand-held. 23 - **Make the zoom asymmetric.** When the shape grows, the camera must pull out quickly (omega 12), or the card spills off the frame for 0.3 s. When the shape shrinks, push in gently (omega 7): it reads as a deliberate push-in. 24 - Keep text crisp: don't set `will-change` on the world or shape (Chrome would scale a cached bitmap), and render at 1x device scale. Every frame is re-rasterised at its own zoom. 25 26 ## The cursor 27 28 - Show a real arrow cursor (black with a white keyline), in screen space so it never scales with the camera. 29 - **Every change is caused:** a click on a button, a drag on a control, a press-and-hold. A state that advances by itself breaks the illusion. 30 - Choreograph it like a person: glance across rows while they reveal (hover highlights follow), travel to the button about 1 s before the click so the hover state reads, then press. On press the cursor shrinks 10% and the target depresses 4% (the whole shape depresses 2.8% if you click the shape itself). 31 - For drags, the control reads the cursor's actual position, so knobs, scrub lines and tooltips are glued to the pointer. 32 - The cursor path is a spring toward each new target: fast start, soft landing. Don't add arcs or overshoot. 33 34 ## Timing and rhythm 35 36 - Use a beat grid (120 BPM → 0.5 s beats, 2 s bars). State lengths are multiples of 0.5 s and big moments sit on bar lines, which is what lets the music hit the cuts. 37 - No dead time: inside a state, something reveals, counts, draws or responds at every moment. If the cursor waits more than about 1 s, tighten the state or give the cursor something to hover. 38 - Stagger reveals at 0.12-0.2 s per item, springs at omega 15-17, zeta 0.84-0.9 for chips and numbers (a hint of overshoot reads as life), zeta 1 for text. 39 40 ## The loop 41 42 - The last state duplicates state 0 (size, fill, zoom, content) and the cursor returns to `cursorHome`. 43 - Two traps the engine now handles; know them in case you write your own: 44 1. The camera lean has its own resting point (lean × cursor home). Start the camera there, not at 0, or frame 0 isn't at rest and the loop jumps. 45 2. The springs need about 1.5 s to fully settle, so the engine pins the last 0.4 s onto frame 0's values. 46 - QA checks the raw seam: SSIM 1.000000 between the rendered frames 0 and N-1. After H.264, expect about 0.99, which is only compression (keyframe versus predicted frame). 47 48 ## Colour and type 49 50 - Use the product's palette. If none is given, use a restrained set: a canvas tint, ink, paper, one brand accent, one success colour, one warning colour. Fill states only from that set. 51 - Use a flat canvas with a faint dot grid in world space. The dots are the only cue that the camera is moving, so keep them subtle. 52 - Use one UI font and tabular numerals for anything that counts. Use Geist Mono (or the product's mono) for receipts, hashes and data. 53 - Draw icons from one set with one stroke weight. Mixing outline sets is the fastest way to look cheap. 54 55 ## Bugs already met (don't repeat them) 56 57 - **A hover tint that resets toggles:** a generic hover routine that set `background = ''` every frame wiped the toggle's "on" colour. Only apply hover tints to the `hover` list; controls own their own colours. 58 - **Odometer overflow:** a template with too few digit columns shows 2.5 for 12.5. Size the template for the largest value. 59 - **SVG presentation attributes don't resolve CSS variables:** `stroke="var(--x)"` fails. Use `style="stroke:var(--x)"`. 60 - **Measurements assume layout at rest:** don't measure elements you transform (scale or translate) in `update`. Measure their static wrappers, or give the cursor offsets from a static element. 61 - **Theme flips mid-reel** (day → night, dark mode): drive the shape with a `fill` function and the canvas, dots and shadow from the `frame` hook, all off one spring channel, so everything crossfades together. 62 - **Real media in content:** put product images (pets, screenshots, logos) in the reel folder and reference them relatively. The engine waits for every `` to load before measuring. 63 - **Headless Chrome screenshots at 390px wide are not a phone:** window sizes have a minimum. For phone framing, lay the scene out at 1080x1920 instead (change `size` and the CSS page size). 64

1	# Score and sound design
2	
3	The music is original and synthesised, so there are no licensing questions. It's built from the reel's own timeline, so it fits the cut exactly. Music-generation tools may be unavailable or restricted to other uses, and this approach doesn't need them.
4	
5	## What the default track is
6	
7	- 120 BPM (matching `bpm`), one chord per bar, cycling `prog` (default F, G, Em, Am in C major: warm, forward, optimistic).
8	- Voices:
9	  - pads: detuned saws through a lowpass that opens and closes by section
10	  - a plucked 16th-note arpeggio of the chord tones, with a dotted-8th delay
11	  - bass: sine plus a quiet triangle an octave up
12	  - kick with sidechain ducking of pads and bass
13	  - offbeat hats, a clap on 2 and 4 in the "lift" sections
14	  - FM bells for motifs
15	  - a noise-and-sine riser
16	  - a sub boom for impacts
17	- The bus runs a 35 Hz high-pass, a gentle compressor (-12 dB threshold, 2.5:1), then peak-normalises. The mux step applies `loudnorm` to -16 LUFS (−1.5 dBTP), which suits social video.
18	- The reverb and delay tail past the end is folded onto the start, so the audio loops as cleanly as the picture.
19	
20	## Sections
21	
22	Sections are chosen per bar. By default:
23	- **intro:** the first 2 bars, soft pads and 8th plucks with no drums.
24	- **groove:** kick, hats, bass, plucks.
25	- **riser:** any bar under a hold. The hats build to 16ths, the bass pulses, the pad opens, and a riser runs until the next state.
26	- **lift:** everything after the first hold. It adds claps, extra hats and a brighter pluck.
27	- **outro:** the last 2 bars, matching the intro so the loop is seamless.
28	- **break:** any bars you list: `breaks: [['trap', 'safe']]` strips it back to a sparse, filtered tension under a "danger" beat, then comes back in on the resolving state.
29	
30	You can also pass `sections: [[0,'intro'],[2,'groove'],[10,'riser'],[11,'lift'],[19,'break'],[22,'lift'],[28,'outro']]`, or a function of the bar.
31	
32	## Shaping it for a product
33	
34	```js
35	score: {
36	  prog: ['F','G','Em','Am', 'F','G','C','C', ...],      // one per bar; land the tonic (C) on the payoff bar
37	  chords: { Bb: { b: 46, p: [58, 62, 65, 69] } },          // add your own voicings (b = bass MIDI, p = pad MIDI)
38	  hits: [{ state: 'done', boom: 0.55, motif: [72, 76, 79] }, { state: 'brand', boom: 0.5, motif: [72, 76, 79, 84] }],
39	  breaks: [['trap', 'safe']],
40	  padCut: { lift: 2000 }, musicLevel: 1, sfxLevel: 0.9,
41	  whooshes: true, clicks: true, holdRiser: true,
42	}
43	```
44	
45	- Put the tonic chord (C) on the bar where the product pays off (confirmation, brand reveal). A V chord (G, or E for tension into Am) on the bar before a big moment makes the arrival feel earned.
46	- Hits: a sub boom plus a rising three-note bell motif on the 2-3 most important moments. More than that and nothing stands out.
47	- Mood: for calmer products, drop the clap (no hold, so no lift) and lower `padCut`. For darker ones, use a minor progression (Am, F, C, G) and hit on Am.
48	
49	## Sound design (`sfx(au, reel)`)
50	
51	The automatic layer gives you a whoosh on every state change (rising when the shape grows, falling when it shrinks) and a tick on every press and release. For scene-specific sounds, use the hook:
52	
53	```js
54	sfx(au, r) {
55	  au.typing(r.at('prompt') + 0.65, r.at('prompt') + 2.6, PROMPT_TEXT);   // a key tick per character
56	  au.detents('slider', 'settings', 0.05);           // a tick each time the slider crosses a 5% step
57	  au.detents('scrub', 'pocket', 1 / 30, 2400, 0.035, (S) => S.scrubOn > 0.5);
58	  au.counter(r.at('pocket') + 0.35, r.at('pocket') + 1.75, 14);   // odometer roll
59	  for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) au.swipe(r.at('trap') + 2.35 + i * 0.17);   // marker redaction swipes
60	  au.bell(r.at('boost') + 1.2, 84, 0.05);
61	}
62	```
63	
64	Available voices: `tick(t, freq, vol, len)`, `whoosh(t, up, vol, len)`, `swipe(t, vol)`, `bell(t, midi, vol)`, `boom(t, vol)`, `riser(t0, t1, vol)`, `typing`, `detents`, `counter`, plus `au.BEAT`, `au.BAR` and `au.at(stateId)`.
65	
66	Keep UI sounds quiet (0.03-0.12). They should be felt under the music, not heard over it.
67	
68	## Checking a mix you can't hear
69	
70	Run `node qa.mjs` and read three things:
71	
72	1. **Loudness range (LRA)** in `summary.txt`. If it's below about 3 LU, the mix is a wall: pads are too loud or the compressor is too hard. The Stockback reel started at 1.5 LU and was fixed to 5.6 by lowering the pads (0.05 to 0.032 per voice) and softening the compressor.
73	2. **`spectrum.png`.** Look for a *sustained* bright band below 40 Hz. Short flashes there at each kick and boom are expected: the kick ends at 52 Hz, the boom at 45 Hz, and a 40 Hz high-pass cleans the rest. The first Stockback mix had the bass sine an octave too low (41-55 Hz fundamentals), which ate the headroom. Phone speakers can't play it anyway. Bass fundamentals belong around 80-130 Hz, plus the 35 Hz high-pass.
74	3. **`wave.png`.** The sections should be visible: a quieter intro and outro, a build under the riser, the breakdown dip, and dense lift sections. If it looks like one flat block, add contrast.
75	
76	Then tell the user plainly that the audio was checked by analysis, not by ear, and invite them to listen.
77

content.text:
The reel is done and sent to you above: **68 seconds, 1080p60 with an original score**, styled after your friend's reel. The file is `video/out/parallax-reel.mp4` (19.6 MB). There's also a 720p copy at `video/out/parallax-reel-720p.mp4` (5.8 MB) if X's upload struggles with the big one.

**What's in it**, every change triggered by the cursor:
1. The Parallax pill opens into a black panel: "Research agents ~~sound sure.~~ Often, they're wrong."
2. A white panel: "What if every answer was checked from two **angles?**", with an orange underline drawn in.
3. Hiring a company brief on Supabase. The text types into the form, then "Get a quote".
4. The CFO quotes $5.00 with a $0.51 hard cap, and you hold to hire.
5. Records and Field side by side on real Supabase facts: two agree, two conflict.
6. The Arbiter's tiebreak on headcount: 439 and 120 get struck through, Supabase's careers page is quoted, and it settles on 350+.
7. The Verifier counts up to 7/7, and the Writer's first draft gets sent back. Then "Delivered".
8. The neatlogs trace tree: "Every step. Every call. Every cent." plus the 429 detection card.
9. The production crash and resume: the steps fill in, "server restarted" appears, and run 2 finishes.
10. The eval proof: 14/14 right, guesswork 39% → 0%, $0.12 → $0.07 per lead.
11. The manifesto, line by line: "Records reads the databases. Field reads the web. Nothing ships *unchecked*."
12. The logo lockup, then "Hire the team" collapses back to the opening pill, so it loops seamlessly.

**Checks:** the loop seam is perfect, the transitions have no muddy frames, and the loudness is −15.4 LUFS with a −2 dBTP peak, which suits X. I checked the audio by analysis, not by ear. I also added a breakdown under the crash beat so the music doesn't sit at one level the whole way. Give it a listen.

I committed the reel's source in `video/` locally as `18d9a5c`, not pushed. One thing to decide before pushing: `reel.js` and `score.js` (the motion engine and its music generator) come from your ui-motion-reel skill, which was written before the hackathon. Pushing them could clash with the "all code written Oct 10–12" rule. If you'd rather not risk it, I'll keep `video/` out of the repo and only link the rendered video.

Want any changes? Shorter for X (around 30 seconds), different wording, more of the agent characters, or a different pace. A re-render takes about 3 minutes.
